newsitem.title: USA: House Banking Committee averts Democratic revolt.
newsitem.headline: House Banking Committee averts Democratic revolt.

text.p: The House Banking Committee's effort to overhaul U.S. banking laws almost came to a standstill late Wednesday, when Republicans sought to reopen debate on an amendment that had passed hours earlier.
But Republicans backed down after Democrats on the committee threatened to reopen votes on all of the dozens of amendments already considered during the day and at a previous session on Tuesday.
At issue was a seemingly minor amendment by California Democrat Maxine Waters to require banks to offer low cost accounts known as "lifeline" accounts.

Under the Waters amendment, a bank could not take advantage of the many new powers granted under the overall bank reform legislation unless the institution showed a "demonstrable record of performance" in providing lifeline accounts.
Under a 1991 law, banks are already given a discount on insurance premiums for offering lifeline accounts, Democratic staffers noted.
The amendment passed on a voice vote with no objections heard.
But the leading bank trade group, the American Bankers Association, immediately went on the attack, phoning lawmakers to voice its objections.

"It's a big, big problem," the group's top lobbyist, Ed Yingling, told reporters outside the hearing room after the amendment was adopted. Republicans on the committee "didn't understand the implications," he added.

Banks feared regulators would turn the one sentence provision into a vast and costly new set of regulations. "We're convinced that provision will eventually turn into a huge regulation on banks," he said.
"If this gets reconsidered, then maybe the others get reconsidered," Frank said.
After a heated debate, McCollum backed down and withdrew his motion. "Obviously we're engendering ill will, which I didn't intend to do by this," he said.
Instead, Republicans will fight the amendment in a subsequent legislative venue, McCollum said. "I think it was a mistake to adopt it but we can deal with it later," he said.
If the banking committee ultimately approves the bill, the legislation then goes to the Commerce Committee for further consideration.
Rep. Waters said after the session that Democrats were prepared to "do guerrilla warfare" if the vote was reconsidered.

"Consumers deserve some consideration in all of this," she said. "Consumers don't have the high paid, ABA-type lobbyist here who give huge campaign contributions to members of this committee doing their bidding."
